question: A team runs a three-node etcd cluster and wants more resilience, so it proposes adding a fourth node. What does the fourth node change?
options: The cluster now tolerates two failures
The majority grows from 2 to 3, so the cluster still tolerates one failure and every write waits for one more acknowledgement
Nothing: Raft ignores even-numbered nodes
Writes become faster because there are more replicas to answer
explanation: Fault tolerance is n minus the majority: 4 - 3 = 1, the same as 3 - 2. To tolerate two failures you need five nodes, where the majority is three.

question: A five-node Raft cluster is split by a partition into a group of two (including the old leader) and a group of three. What happens?
options: Both groups keep accepting writes and merge them later
Neither group can accept writes until the partition heals
The group of three elects a new leader in a higher term and commits writes; the old leader cannot commit because it cannot reach a majority
The old leader keeps committing because it was elected first
explanation: Committing and electing both need a majority of 3. Only the larger side has one, so it elects a leader with a higher term; the old leader's new entries never reach a majority and are discarded when it rejoins.

question: Node C (last log entry: term 5, index 12) asks node A (last entry: term 6, index 7) for a vote in term 7. A has not voted in term 7. What does A do?
options: Refuses: A's last entry has a higher term, so C's log is less up-to-date even though it is longer
Grants: C's log is longer
Grants: A has not voted in this term
Refuses: candidates may only ask for votes in their own term
explanation: The up-to-date check compares the last log term first and uses the index only to break ties. A term-6 entry may be committed, and electing C could erase it.

question: All followers of a cluster use the same fixed election timeout. After the leader crashes, elections keep failing. Why?
options: Raft forbids elections after a crash
Fixed timeouts make heartbeats too slow
The term number overflows
The followers time out together, all become candidates, vote for themselves and split the vote, again and again
explanation: Randomized election timeouts make one follower usually time out first and collect a majority before the others start. With identical timeouts candidates collide and no one reaches a majority.

question: A new leader in term 4 finds an entry from term 2 stored on a majority of nodes. May it mark that entry committed right away?
options: Yes: any entry stored on a majority is committed
No: entries from earlier terms are committed only once an entry from the current term after them reaches a majority
Yes, but only if the entry is the last one in the log
No: entries from earlier terms are always deleted by a new leader
explanation: A previous-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten by a later leader that never saw it. Raft commits by counting only for current-term entries, which commits everything before them at the same time.

question: A lock service elects a leader that writes to shared storage. The old leader pauses for a long garbage collection, wakes up and tries to write. What stops it from corrupting data?
options: A longer election timeout
Retrying the write with exponential backoff
A fencing token such as the term: storage rejects any write carrying a token lower than one it has already seen
A fourth replica in the cluster
explanation: A paused node cannot know it lost leadership. Fencing makes the storage enforce the order: the new leader's higher token was seen, so the stale leader's lower token is refused.
